title: Sangiovese
description: Also called Brunello, Prugnolo Gentile and Morellino in Tuscany. Italy's most planted red: sour cherry, high acidity and firm tannin.
L: Sangiovese gives medium-bodied reds with sour cherry, red plum, tomato leaf, dried herbs and, with age, leather and earth. Acidity is high, tannins firm and often slightly drying, like strong tea. Colour is medium ruby, fading early to garnet. It's Italy's most planted grape.
Sour cherry, high acidity, tea-like tannin

Sangiovese may come from sanguis Jovis, Latin for the blood of Jupiter. DNA shows it's a cross of Ciliegiolo and Calabrese di Montenuovo, linking Tuscany and the south. It's genetically unstable, with many clones: Sangiovese Grosso, with bigger berries, is used in Montalcino, where it's called Brunello.
What does Sangiovese's name possibly mean?
Sanguis Jovis, Latin for the blood of Jupiter.

Look for medium ruby or garnet colour, often with an orange tint even when quite young. On the nose, sour cherry, herbs and earth. On the palate, high acidity and grainy, drying tannin. That combination of sour cherry and tea-like tannin, plus the urge to eat something with tomato, is the clue.
Sangiovese is usually deeply coloured and low in acidity.
Not true. It's medium in colour and high in acidity.
Sangiovese gives sour cherry, herbs and earth
It has high acidity and firm, tea-like tannin
It's Italy's most planted grape, with many clones
Explain the climate and soils it needs

Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany: Chianti, Montalcino, Montepulciano, Carmignano and Morellino di Scansano. It also grows in Umbria, Romagna, the Marche and Lazio. Outside Italy, it's planted in Corsica, as Nielluccio, California, Argentina and Australia, but rarely with the same success.

Sangiovese ripens late and needs warmth, but too much heat makes it flat and jammy. It shows best on hillsides at 250 to 600 m, with good sun and cool nights. Galestro, a crumbly marl schist, and alberese, a hard limestone, give its finest wines. It's prone to rot in wet autumns because of its thin skins.
Match each regional name to its place.
Sangiovese takes local names in its best zones.

Across the Apennines, Romagna makes Sangiovese di Romagna, now Romagna Sangiovese DOC, often fruitier and softer. Its sub-zones, like Predappio and Modigliana, are making more serious wines. It shows that Sangiovese isn't only Tuscan.
Which soils give Sangiovese's finest wines in Tuscany?
Galestro marl and alberese limestone are prized in Chianti Classico.
Sangiovese is the soul of Tuscany, also grown across central Italy
It needs warm hillsides and cool nights
Galestro and alberese give its finest wines
Explain the difference between Chianti and Chianti Classico
Describe its rules and quality levels

Chianti covers a large area across Tuscany, with seven sub-zones like Rufina and Colli Senesi. Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, the original zone between Florence and Siena, defined in 1716 by Cosimo III de' Medici. Classico must be at least 80% Sangiovese; white grapes were banned in 2006.
Chianti Classico: a separate, original zone

Chianti Classico has three levels: Annata, the basic wine; Riserva, aged at least 24 months; and Gran Selezione, created in 2014, from estate-grown grapes aged at least 30 months. Since 2021, Gran Selezione needs at least 90% Sangiovese, and labels can name 11 villages, called UGAs, like Radda and Panzano.
Chianti Classico's top level, created in 2014, is called ____.
Gran Selezione sits above Riserva and Annata, with estate grapes and at least 30 months of ageing.

The black rooster, gallo nero, is Chianti Classico's symbol. Legend says Florence and Siena settled their border with a race: riders left at the first cockcrow. Florence's black rooster, starved, crowed early, so its rider got further. Every Chianti Classico bottle carries it on the neck.
Chianti and Chianti Classico are the same DOCG.
Not true. Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, the original historic zone.
Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, defined in 1716
It has Annata, Riserva and Gran Selezione
The black rooster marks every bottle

Montalcino, a hill town south of Siena, is warmer and drier than Chianti. Brunello di Montalcino, DOCG since 1980, must be 100% Sangiovese and age at least five years, two in oak, before release; Riserva six years. The Biondi-Santi family created the style in the late 19th century. Rosso di Montalcino is the younger, cheaper version.

Montepulciano, east of Montalcino, makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG from at least 70% Sangiovese, locally called Prugnolo Gentile. It ages at least two years. It's often softer than Brunello and more structured than Chianti. Not to be confused with Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, a different grape and region.
What does Brunello di Montalcino require?
Brunello is pure Sangiovese, aged at least five years before release.

Chianti Classico is often the freshest, with sour cherry and violet. Brunello, from a warmer place and with longer ageing, is fuller, more powerful and long-lived. Vino Nobile sits between them. All three show Sangiovese's acidity and tannin.
Match each wine to its rule.
Each Tuscan wine sets its own rules.
Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, aged five years
Vino Nobile is at least 70% Prugnolo Gentile
Brunello is fullest; Chianti Classico freshest
Explain how the Super Tuscans began
Explain their effect on Italian law

In the 1960s and 1970s, Chianti rules required white grapes in the blend and limited international grapes. Some producers wanted to make the best wine they could instead. Sassicaia, first sold in 1971, used Cabernet Sauvignon. Tignanello, in 1971, blended Sangiovese with Cabernet in small barrels, with no white grapes.

Because they broke DOC rules, these wines had to be sold as Vino da Tavola, the lowest category, yet sold for more than any Chianti. The press named them Super Tuscans. In 1992, Italy created IGT to give them a category; Sassicaia got its own DOC in 2013. Chianti Classico's rules changed too.
The first Super Tuscans had to be labelled as simple table wine.
Yes. Breaking DOC rules meant they could only be sold as Vino da Tavola.

Super Tuscans include Sangiovese-based wines, like Flaccianello and Pergole Torte, which is pure Sangiovese, and Bordeaux blends from Bolgheri, like Ornellaia. Many use small French oak. Since Chianti Classico now allows 100% Sangiovese, some producers have returned to the DOCG.
Barolo is a Piedmont DOCG made from Nebbiolo.
Super Tuscans broke DOC rules in the 1970s
They led to the IGT category in 1992
They include Sangiovese and Bordeaux-style wines

Sangiovese's acidity makes it perfect with tomato: pasta al pomodoro, pizza, lasagne. Its tannin suits grilled meat, like bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick T-bone. Brunello suits wild boar, game and aged pecorino. It's one of the most food-dependent reds; it can taste austere alone.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Chianti Classico Annata is best within five years. Riserva and Gran Selezione age 10 to 20 years. Brunello ages 15 to 30 years, gaining leather, tobacco and dried cherry. Decant young Brunello.
A classic Tuscan match for Chianti or Brunello.
If a Sangiovese tastes austere on its own, try it with a bite of tomato pasta. Its acidity and tannin will suddenly make sense.
Sweet desserts make it taste sour.
Its tannin suits grilled meat and aged cheese
Match each wine to its description.
Sangiovese has several great Tuscan expressions.
Which soils are prized for Sangiovese in Chianti Classico?
The IGT category was created partly because of the Super Tuscans.
Brunello di Montalcino must age at least ____ years before release.
Five years, two of them in oak; Riserva needs six.
Sangiovese is high in acidity, with sour cherry and firm tannin
Chianti Classico, Brunello and Vino Nobile are its great wines
Super Tuscans broke rules and changed Italian law
It's made for tomato and grilled meat
